'''Mark A. O'Neill''' is an English [[computational biology|computational biologist]] with interests in [[artificial intelligence]], [[systems biology]], [[complex systems]] and [[image analysis]]. He is the creator and lead programmer on a number of computational projects including the [[Digital Automated Identification SYstem (DAISY)]] for [[automated species identification]] and [[PUPS P3]], an [[organic computing]] environment for [[Linux]].

==Education==
O'Neill was educated at [[The King's School, Grantham]], [[Sheffield University]] and [[University College London]].<ref>{{cite thesis
|last=O'Neill
|first=Mark A.
|year=1992
|title=Kinematic Model of the SPOT-1 Sensor
|publisher=University College London
}}</ref>

==Research interests==
O'Neill's interests lie at the interface of biology and computing. He has worked in the areas of [[artificial life]] and [[biologically inspired computing]]. In particular, he has attempted to answer the question "can one create [[software agents]] which are capable of carrying a useful computational payload which respond to their environment with the flexibility of a living [[organism]]?"

He has also investigated how computational methods may be used to analyze biological and quasi biological systems for example: [[ecosystem]]s and [[economies]].

O'Neill is also interested in [[ethology]], especially the emergent social ecosystems which occur as a result of [[social networking]] on the [[internet]]. His recent projects include the use of artificial intelligence techniques to look at complex socio-economic data.<ref>{{cite journal
|first1=Elizabeth |last1=Lloyd Parkes
|first2=Robert I. W. |last2=Lang
|first3=Mark A. |last3=O'Neill
|title=Understanding Tweens" Identity as Expressed through Conspicuous Consumption: an Adaptive Neural Net Approach to the Analysis of a Complex Socio-Economic Dataset
|url=https://www.tumblingdice.co.uk/documents/ComplexApproach.pdf
|date=24 April 2008
|publisher=Tumbling Dice
|journal=Child and Teen Consumption – Conference on Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Child and Teen Consumption
|location=Trondheim, Norway
}}</ref>

On the computer science front, O'Neill continues to develop and contribute to a number of other [[Open-source model|open source]] and commercial software projects and is involved in the design of cluster/parallel computer hardware via his company, [https://www.tumblingdice.co.uk  Tumbling Dice Ltd]. Long-running projects include DAISY;<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Reed
|first1=Sarah
|date=25 June 2010
|title=Pushing Daisy
|journal=Science
|volume=328
|pages=1628–1629
|doi=10.1126/science.328.5986.1628
|pmid=20576867
|issue=5986
}}</ref>
PUPS P3 an organic computing environment for Linux; [[Cryopid]], a Linux process freezer; the [https://www.tumblingdice.co.uk/mensor &#91;Mensor digital terrain model generation system&#93;]; and [[RanaVision]], a vision based motion detection system. He has also worked with public domain agent based social interaction models such as [[Sugarscape]] and artificial life simulators, for example physis, which is a development of [[Tierra (computer simulation)|Tierra]].

O'Neill has been a keen naturalist since childhood. In addition to his interests in complex systems and computer science, he is a member of the [[Royal Entomological Society]] and an expert in the rearing and ecology of [[hawk moth]]s. He is also currently convenor of the [https://www.royensoc.co.uk/special-interest-groups/electronic-computing-technology &#91;Electronic and Computing Technology Special Interest Group&#93;] (SIG) for the Royal Entomological Society.

He is also interested in the use of [[precision agriculture]] methodologies to monitor agri-[[ecosystems]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tumblingdice.co.uk/documents/ctrap.pdf|title=Camera Traps|publisher=Tumbling Dice|date=19 September 2010|accessdate=19 December 2010}}</ref> and has been an active participant in a series of projects looking at the automatic tracking of [[Bombus terrestris|bumblebees]],<ref name="BBC">{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/5215022.stm |title=Homing instinct of bees surprises |work=BBC News |date=2006-07-26 |first=Louisa | last=Cheung|accessdate=19 December 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Ian |last=Sample |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2006/jul/26/conservationandendangeredspecies.uknews |title=The flight of the bumblebee is measured at record eight miles |newspaper=The Guardian |date=26 July 2006 |accessdate=14 June 2012}}</ref> and other insects<ref name="ITV">{{cite video|url=https://www.tumblingdice.co.uk/movies/tracking.html|title=Tracking Bombus terrestris (ITV Tyne Tees)
|accessdate=19 December 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|last1=O’Neill
|first1=M.A.
|last2=Barlow
|first2=S
|last3=Port
|first3=G. P. 
|year=2010
|title=Recording pollinator visitation to ''Rhinanthus minor'' (Hay rattle) using an automated motion sensitive detection system 
|journal=Entomology 2010
|publisher=University of Swansea
}}</ref> using vision, and using both [[Network theory|network analysis]] and [[remote sensing]] techniques to monitor ecosystem health. Latterly, he has become interested in applying these techniques in the commercial sphere to look at issues of [[corporate responsibility]] and [[sustainability]] in industries like mining and agriculture which have significant ecological footprints.

He has also been involved in both [[computational neuroscience]] and [[systems biology]], the former association resulting in many papers while working at [[Oxford University]]. Work in the latter area led to the successful flotation in 2007 of a systems biology company, e-Therapeutics, where O'Neill was a senior scientist, assisted with the establishment of the company, and was named in a number of seminal [[patent]]s.

O'Neill is a fellow of the [[British Computer Society]], the [[Institute of Engineering and Technology]], and the [[Royal Astronomical Society]]. He is also a [[Chartered Engineer (UK)|chartered engineer]], a [[Chartered IT Professional|chartered IT professional]] and a member of the [[Institute of Directors]]. He was one of the recipients of the ''BCS Award for Computing Technology'' in 1992.
